title: Parsing log lines: putting it together
explanation:
Real parsing combines everything: **anchors** to match the whole line, **classes and quantifiers** with exact widths for each field, **named groups** for the fields you want back, and **alternation** for a fixed vocabulary such as log levels. Build the pattern one field at a time and test each addition against a good line and a bad one.

To pull *every* occurrence of a field out of a line, use a global regex with `matchAll`. It returns an iterator of all matches, each including its capture groups — something `match` with `g` can't give you. `matchAll` throws a `TypeError` if the regex lacks the `g` flag.

```js
const line = "cc: ana@home bo@work";
for (const m of line.matchAll(/(\w+)@(\w+)/g)) console.log(m[1], m[2]);  // ana home / bo work
```

One real-world trap: a regex with the `g` (or `y`) flag is **stateful**. It stores `lastIndex`, the position where the next search starts, and `test()`/`exec()` update it. Reusing the same global regex object across different strings can therefore make `test()` alternate between `true` and `false`. Use a non-global regex for yes/no checks, reset `lastIndex = 0`, or use `matchAll`, which works on an internal copy.
keyIdeas: Anchor the whole line; give each field an exact class and width.
Named groups document the fields you extract.
`matchAll` (requires `g`) yields every match with its groups.
Global regexes keep `lastIndex` state — don't reuse them for `test()`.

workedExample.problem: Parse an access-log request like `"GET /docs/index.html HTTP/1.1 404 512"` into method, path, status, and bytes. Reject `"FETCH /x HTTP/1.1 200 5"` (unknown method) and `"GET /x HTTP/1.1 20 5"` (status must be 3 digits).
steps: Method is a fixed vocabulary → alternation in a named group: `(?<method>GET|POST|PUT|DELETE)`.
The path is a run of non-spaces: `(?<path>\S+)`. The protocol is literal text with escaped `/` and `.`: `HTTP\/\d\.\d`.
Status is exactly three digits `(?<status>\d{3})`; bytes is one or more digits `(?<bytes>\d+)`.
Join the fields with single spaces and anchor with `^...$` so malformed lines fail instead of half-matching.
workedExample.answer: `{ method: "GET", path: "/docs/index.html", status: "404", bytes: "512" }`; both malformed lines return `null`.

pitfalls: Leaving the pattern unanchored, so a malformed line still "matches" a fragment and produces wrong fields.
Reusing one `/.../g` regex for `test()` on many strings and getting alternating results because of `lastIndex`.
Using `.*` for fields; a greedy `.*` can swallow the separators of later fields.

citations.quote: The matchAll() method of String values returns an iterator of all results matching this string against a regular expression, including capturing groups.
If regexp is a regex, then it must have the global (g) flag set, or a TypeError is thrown.
The lastIndex data property of a RegExp instance specifies the index at which to start the next match.
This property is set only if the regular expression instance used the g flag to indicate a global search, or the y flag to indicate a sticky search.
console.log(re.test("foo baz")); // false, because lastIndex is non-zero
remember to reset lastIndex after each input is completely processed.
matchAll internally makes a clone of the regexp — so, unlike regexp.exec(), lastIndex does not change as the string is scanned.
Named capturing group: Matches "x" and stores it on the groups property of the returned matches under the name specified by <Name>.
